text:
The word for "nostrils" in that verse, *ʾaph* ("nostril, face, anger"), is also the ordinary Hebrew word for anger, and for the face. To be patient is to be "long of nostrils". God uses the same phrase of himself: "slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6).
- The same word is used for the face bowed to the ground in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3).
- It is used for the face lifted in pride: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him" (Psalm 10:4).

Life is set before the inner being as something to choose. "I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live" (Deuteronomy 30:19). The same chapter also speaks of God's own work on the heart: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live" (30:6). The choice is made by doing, seeking and holding on:
- "if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the Lord" (Leviticus 18:5)
- "Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live" (Deuteronomy 16:20)
- "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live" (Proverbs 4:4)
- "Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight" (Proverbs 9:6)
- "Seek me and live" (Amos 5:4); "Seek good, and not evil, that you may live" (5:14)
- "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4)

The one before whom life is lived is called "the living God". The name sets him against idols: "But the Lord is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King" (Jeremiah 10:10); "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Habakkuk mocks the other side: "Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him" (Habakkuk 2:19–20). What has no breath cannot be woken, and the one who calls on it "trusts in his own creation" (2:18). Before the living God, the answer is silence.

Sin can be put away while a death still follows. Nathan says to David, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the Lord, the child who is born to you shall die" (2 Samuel 12:13–14).

Sheol is never full. "Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man" (Proverbs 27:20). It heads the list of things that "never say, 'Enough'" (30:15–16). "Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure" (Isaiah 5:14); the word for its appetite is *nephesh* ("soul, appetite"). Sinners invite a son to join them: "like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole" (Proverbs 1:12). The same picture is used of people. Proverbs sets the eyes of man beside Sheol, and Habakkuk the arrogant man: "His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Habakkuk 2:5).

A death is met by those who remain, and Scripture shows them.
- Hagar could not watch: "Let me not look on the death of the child." And "she lifted up her voice and wept" (Genesis 21:16).
- David fasted and wept while his child was ill. When the child died, he "arose and ate food", and his servants asked why. He answered, "But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Samuel 12:21, 23).
- His grief for Absalom brought Joab's rebuke: "today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased" (2 Samuel 19:6).
- Martha met Jesus with, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (John 11:21).
- At Nain a dead man was carried out, "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow". Jesus raised him and "gave him to his mother" (Luke 7:12, 15).
- Paul was spared a death he feared: God had mercy on Epaphroditus, "and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow" (Philippians 2:27).
- Uriah's wife "lamented over her husband" (2 Samuel 11:26). Jacob speaks of Rachel's death, "to my sorrow" (Genesis 48:7).

Others hold to someone, or to something, even to death.
- Ruth to Naomi: "Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried" (Ruth 1:17).
- The spies to Rahab: "Our life for yours even to death!" (Joshua 2:14).
- Jonathan, condemned by his father's oath: "Here I am; I will die" (1 Samuel 14:43).
- Esther, going to the king: "if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16).
- Thomas: "Let us also go, that we may die with him" (John 11:16).
- Job: "till I die I will not put away my integrity from me" (Job 27:5).
- Paul: "I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting" (1 Corinthians 9:15).
- To a church: "Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). Of the faithful: "they loved not their lives even unto death" (Revelation 12:11).

These are prophetic oracles. Jesus also tells of two men after death, and the one who is buried is aware and speaks:
- "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side" (Luke 16:22–23).
- He cries, "I am in anguish in this flame". Abraham answers, "Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things … but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish", and "between us and you a great chasm has been fixed" (16:24–26).
- He asks for his five brothers, and is told, "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead" (16:28–31).

section: The heart decides and is moved
text:
The verses on willing name the heart beside the will again and again (10.7, *Willing*).
- **A willing heart gives.** "All who were of a willing heart brought" (Exodus 35:22). After consecration, "all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings" (2 Chronicles 29:31).
- **A hardened heart will not.** "But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go" (Exodus 10:27). Of Sihon: "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30).
- **A stubborn heart will not listen.** "the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart" (Ezekiel 3:7). And when Israel would not submit, "I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (Psalm 81:12).
- **A melted heart will not go.** "Yet you would not go up" (Deuteronomy 1:26), because "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (1:28).
- **A heart that blesses itself.** "I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart" (Deuteronomy 29:19). Of that man, "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him" (29:20).
- **A heart lifted up.** Nebuchadnezzar's will was absolute, "Whom he would, he killed" (Daniel 5:19), "But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (5:20). His son "knew all this", and Daniel says to him, "you … have not humbled your heart" (5:22).
  - The words of that heart are given earlier: "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?" "While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven" (Daniel 4:30–31). He had been told that his kingdom would be confirmed "from the time that you know that Heaven rules" (4:26). I read the boast as that heart speaking.
- **A heart not right, wanting power.** Simon offered money: "Give me this power also". Peter: "your heart is not right before God … pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you" (Acts 8:19, 21–22).
- **Hearts inclined by kinship.** Abimelech asked the men of Shechem to choose one ruler over seventy, "Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh", and "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3).
- **No one comes near of his own heart.** Of the ruler to come: "I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 30:21). The words rendered "dare of himself" carry the word for the heart. The nearness is God's doing.

The heart is named **just before** the anger, in the state it was in when the anger came.
- Haman "went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (Esther 5:9).
- "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16). The Hebrew has *his heart was lifted up*. Three verses later Uzziah's anger at the priests breaks out with leprosy (26:19).

The angry can **read another's heart wrongly**. Eliab, angry at David on the battlefield: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle" (1 Samuel 17:28). The chapter shows David was sent by his father with food (17:17–18, 20).

Under God's anger, the verses give the heart several roles, each in its own verses.
- **The heart that provokes it.** "And the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the Lord" (1 Kings 11:9). "Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah" (Psalm 95:8). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came from the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 7:12). "Because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The heart that turns it.** "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us" (2 Chronicles 29:10). "But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart … so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Josiah was heard "because your heart was penitent" (2 Kings 22:19).
- **The heart that is called to be torn, or cut.** "Return to me with all your heart … and rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord; remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (Jeremiah 4:4).
- **The heart that does not take it in.** "It set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **The heart that rejoices** when God's anger acts for it: "You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice … and the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies" (Isaiah 66:14).

The heart is where a person humbles himself. "Because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the Lord" (2 Kings 22:19); in the parallel account, "your heart was tender" (2 Chronicles 34:27). "If then their uncircumcised heart is humbled" (Leviticus 26:41). Hezekiah "humbled himself for the pride of his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:26), the same heart that was proud a verse before (32:25). Daniel "set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God" (Daniel 10:12). Belshazzar's charge is the refusal: "you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this" (Daniel 5:22).

God humbles too, and what he reaches is the heart: "testing you to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2); "he bowed their hearts down with hard labor" (Psalm 107:12). The opposite is named: "Before destruction a man's heart is haughty" (Proverbs 18:12).

"learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). The rest is promised to the soul, and it is found by learning from one who is lowly in heart. The word received with meekness "is able to save your souls" (James 1:21). Leaders are to be obeyed because "they are keeping watch over your souls" (Hebrews 13:17). And the soul boasts in the Lord, not in itself: "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psalm 34:2). Humility is in 10.14.

**It is lowly or proud, and it is judged.** "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse chooses the company: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19). "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Proverbs 29:23). "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). God dwells "with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Israel was "a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). The psalm's blessed man is "the one whose transgression is forgiven" (Psalm 32:1), the man "against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit" (32:2). The no-deceit stands beside his confession: "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity" (32:5). David prays for "a right spirit" (Psalm 51:10). Paul calls for cleansing "from every defilement of body and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). And "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Proverbs 16:2).

This matters because it is often said that the human spirit never sins. It is true that I found no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin". But the spirit is certainly judged. It is proud or lowly, faithful or unfaithful, deceitful or clean, and it needs renewing.

**In anger it is held back, heated, pressed and embittered.** The wisdom sayings speak of the spirit in an anger as something kept cool or let run: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (Ecclesiastes 7:8), and "he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding" (Proverbs 17:27). "He who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Proverbs 14:29) is literally short of spirit. In the accounts, the spirit is named in other ways.
- **Provoked:** Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). What followed was reasoning: "So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews" (17:17).
- **Pressed until it speaks:** Elihu "burned with anger" (Job 32:2), waited, and then said, "the spirit within me constrains me" (32:18), and "I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:20).
- **Embittered, with the lips rash:** at Meribah "they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33). The verse does not say whether the spirit is Moses' or God's.
- **Receiving God's anger:** "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison" (Job 6:4).
- **What would faint,** and so is the reason God's anger is held back: "For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). Moses pleaded on the same ground: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Numbers 16:22).

**It is stirred, and it is hardened.** "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (Ezra 1:1). The returning exiles were "everyone whose spirit God had stirred" (Ezra 1:5). Not everyone went; the stirred ones rose. Haggai shows what came before the stirring. The people "obeyed the voice of the Lord … And the people feared the Lord", and they were told "I am with you". Then "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel … and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house" (Haggai 1:12–14). The same chapter had them sowing much and harvesting little, clothed and not warm (1:6; 10.6). The spirit is stirred toward destroying too: "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" after his people "broke faith" (1 Chronicles 5:25–26), and "the spirit of the kings of the Medes" against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11). 13.1 (*Stirring*) gathers what the verses say of God in this. And of Sihon: "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30), the same verse saying that he "would not let us pass by him". Nebuchadnezzar's spirit hardened itself with his pride: "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (Daniel 5:20).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
text: - "The desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
text:
The same letters say what is to be done with these desires. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (5:24). "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). Peter speaks of living "for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:2). In that verse "the flesh" is simply life in the body, and the passions are what it is no longer lived for. The same desires can be used on others. False teachers "entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error" (2 Peter 2:18); they "indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority" (2:10). And flesh can be an outward mark to boast in: "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised", and "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Galatians 6:12–13).
Jude sets the same acts together: "relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones" (Jude 8). Against them he sets the archangel, who "did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you'" (9; 13.2). They "blaspheme all that they do not understand" (10).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
text: Here flesh is spoken of as having desires and a mind: it wants, it sets its mind, it judges "according to the flesh" (John 8:15), and it boasts "according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 11:18).

- It **testifies**: "their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Romans 2:15). "My conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 9:1). "Our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience" (2 Corinthians 1:12).
- "Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart [bosom] the insults of all the many nations" (Psalm 89:50).

section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
text: **"The soul sins; the human spirit never does."** It is true that "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but there the soul means the *person*, the one who answers for the sin. And while I find no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin", the spirit is plainly judged. It is "haughty" before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). It was "not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). It is hardened (Deuteronomy 2:30). It needs to be made "right" (Psalm 51:10). It has or lacks "deceit" (Psalm 32:2). It needs cleansing from "defilement" (2 Corinthians 7:1). If Scripture has a *moral centre*, it is the heart (Chapter 12). The spirit stands beside it, not above it.

It rises where a heart that was lifted up is checked. Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2 Chronicles 26:16). When the priests withstood him, "Uzziah was angry" (26:19). The king's anger burned when "the heart of the king was merry with wine" and his queen refused him (Esther 1:10–12). Chapter 11 follows this threshold further.

The words for delight name what a person takes pleasure in, and the verses show delight set on many things. What it is set on tells what the person is.
- **On God's word, against a heart that has stopped feeling:** "their heart is unfeeling like fat, but I delight in your law" (Psalm 119:70). A few verses on, the same delight is held in the psalmist's own affliction: "I know, O Lord, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me … Let your mercy come to me, that I may live; for your law is my delight" (119:75, 77). In the first it stands against other people's dullness. In the second it stands against his own pain, and he gives it as his ground for asking for mercy.
- **On what satisfies, by invitation:** "Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food" (Isaiah 55:2).
- **On oneself, even in worship:** "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers" (Isaiah 58:3; 10.7).
- **Missing where it belongs:** "A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in expressing his opinion" (Proverbs 18:2).
- **On another's harm:** "let those be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt!" (Psalm 40:14; 70:2).
- **On war and on taking:** "Trample underfoot those who lust after tribute; scatter the peoples who delight in war" (Psalm 68:30). The verse before says "kings shall bear gifts to you" (68:29), and the verse after, "Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God" (68:31). I read the psalm setting delight that feeds on taking and on conflict beside giving and coming.
- **On scoffing:** *"How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge?"* (Proverbs 1:22), said by Wisdom as she calls.

section: On God's word, and on God
text:
Delight set on God himself comes, in these verses, after something else has been let go.
- **After envy.** "Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever" (Psalm 73:25–26). The same man had said, "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3).
- **After one's own pleasure.** "If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day … then you shall take delight in the Lord" (Isaiah 58:13–14).
- **In peace.** "But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace" (Psalm 37:11), in the psalm that says "Delight yourself in the Lord" (37:4; 10.6). The meek are in 10.14.

section: When delight is only the measure
text: | "they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10) | ears that cannot listen; the word scorned | 10.2 |

section: When delight is only the measure
text: | "for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8) | mockery | 10.5 |

Ears can be closed to a word that is still being spoken. "To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10). The act is a hearing that does not happen. "Cannot listen" is followed by what they do with the word instead: they scorn it. Taking no pleasure in it is the measure of the scorn. I read the uncircumcised ears as hearing that lacks the mark of belonging to him. The one who must speak is left holding it: "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (6:11).

Learning to fear God takes a life. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The ear decides much: "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise" (Proverbs 15:31). God can open the ear himself. In a dream "he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Delivered from death") gives the setting.

Wisdom, refused, says: "I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Proverbs 1:26). And "whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster" (1:33).

Receiving a word can wait on being willing. "and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:14–15). The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:11–12). Paul calls a saying "trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The other way is also named: scoffers "following their own sinful desires … deliberately overlook this fact" (2 Peter 3:3, 5). I read the willing, or the unwilling, as standing before the hearing in these verses.

In several of these scenes, perplexity ends when someone comes.
- The two men at the tomb (Luke 24:4).
- To the perplexed chief priests, "someone came and told them, 'Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people'" (Acts 5:24–25).
- At Peter's gate, the men from Cornelius, and then the Spirit: "the Spirit said to him, 'Behold, three men are looking for you'" (Acts 10:17, 19).
- Peter "lifted up his voice" to the crowd (Acts 2:14).
- The queen named Daniel, in whom "an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found" (Daniel 5:12).

section: Remembering as a cure, and remembering as hope
text:
So remembering is commanded.
- **Against self-righteousness:** "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (Deuteronomy 9:7). It comes straight after "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (9:4).
- **Against fear:** "you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:18).
- **Against the pride of having:** "You shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:18).
- **Kept in a song**, so it will not be lost: "this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring)" (Deuteronomy 31:21).

The same skill is put to different uses:
- The tabernacle craftsmen were given it for God's house (Exodus 35:35). Huram-abi, sent to Solomon for the temple, was trained "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2 Chronicles 2:14). His skill was to carry out a design another gave him.
- King Uzziah's engineers turned it to war: "he made machines, invented by skillful men … And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:15). The next verse: "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (26:16).
- Those "at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1) turned it on themselves: they "like David invent for themselves instruments of music" (6:5).

Being reckoned is felt from the inside.
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22).
- "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3).
- A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9).
- Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13).
- A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).

**It reasons, inside and between.** The Greek word for reasoning is used for a single heart talking to itself and for people talking together, with no change of word.
- Inside: a thought can be a whole sentence. "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17).
- Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).

**One word, three faces: *mᵊzimmāh*.**
- In the young it is discretion: "to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth" (Proverbs 1:4). It "will watch over you" (2:11).
- In the wicked it is an evil device, joined to arrogance: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2). It sits beside a short temper: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated" (Proverbs 14:17).
- In God it is purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2). His anger serves it, and it is understood only later: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20).

Anger does not stay a feeling. It starts to reckon, and it reckons badly.
- It reads another's heart, and misreads it. Eliab, angry at his young brother, says, "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart" (1 Samuel 17:28). The reader knows David came because his father sent him.
- It calculates the future. "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" (1 Samuel 18:8). Seventeen verses later it has become a plan: "Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (18:25).
- It soothes itself with a plan. "Your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you" (Genesis 27:42).
- Rage and plotting stand in one line: "Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain?" (Psalm 2:1). The apostles read that psalm over what was done to Jesus (Acts 4:25–27).

Some of what comes out has no words yet. *Hāgāh* is also the sound of grief: "Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove" (Isaiah 38:14). The same word is used of mourning over an enemy. Of proud Moab, whose "boasts are false" (Jeremiah 48:30), the prophet says, "Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn" (Jeremiah 48:31). And it is used of God himself, as a lion that "growls over his prey" and is "not terrified" by the shepherds who come against him (Isaiah 31:4). Idols have no such voice: "they do not make a sound in their throat" (Psalm 115:7).

Mockery can begin without words. "All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads" (Psalm 22:7), and then the words: "He trusts in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (22:8). The mouth and the head move first. The words that follow turn his trust and God's delight into a taunt. He answers God, not them: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9; 13.1).

The servant of Isaiah is the opposite case: *"he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men"* (Isaiah 53:2–3). The woman's look at the tree found something "to be desired" and took it. This look found nothing to desire and turned away. I read that the one who *"has borne our griefs"* (53:4) is the one the desiring eye passed over.

section: Aimed at nothing, and enjoyment given
text: The same words are condemned elsewhere. The rich fool says to his soul, "Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry" (Luke 12:19), and God says, "Fool! This night your soul is required of you" (12:20). The verses themselves show what differs. He says it to his own soul, and it rests on goods laid up and years he presumes to own. The Preacher says it before God, and it rests on a lot received and "the few days … that God has given". Chapter 11 (§4) sets it among the words that change character.

Desire can be pictured as heat and as a drive that no one holds back. Israel going after the Baals is "a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust?" (Jeremiah 2:24). The people answer, "It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go" (2:25). Isaiah uses the same heat: "you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys" (Isaiah 57:5). Just before it come the mocking mouth and the tongue stuck out (57:4). The burning is for other gods, and it reaches as far as the children. In both prophets the heat is for idols, and in both it will not be restrained. Jeremiah ties the heat to fullness: *"When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery … They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife"* (Jeremiah 5:7–8). The same is said of Jeshurun, who *"grew fat, and kicked"* (13.1, *Jealousy*). Fullness, then turning away; and the picture makes the desire animal and loud.

section: Wanting that owns the one who wants
text: The verses give desire the verbs of a person acting on the one who wants. It is obeyed under sin as king: *"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions"* (Romans 6:12). It is followed: *"grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires"* (Jude 16); *"scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming?'"* (2 Peter 3:3–4). It picks what is heard: *"having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths"* (2 Timothy 4:3–4). The itch is a want to be scratched, and the teachers are gathered to scratch it. It keeps learning from arriving: *"led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth"* (3:6–7). It deceives: *"your old self … is corrupt through deceitful desires"* (Ephesians 4:22). It baits: *"each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire"* (James 1:14). That is the fisherman's or hunter's picture, and it comes before the conceiving of 1:15. It takes captive: *"the treacherous are taken captive by their lust"* (Proverbs 11:6). It crouches like an animal at the threshold: *"sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it"* (Genesis 4:7). And it can be inherited: *"You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires"* (John 8:44). I read these as one act seen from different sides: the want leads, and the one who wants follows.

section: Wanting that owns the one who wants
text: What the verses set against it is not a stronger want either. In two places the uncontrolled desire stands beside not knowing God: *"not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God"* (1 Thessalonians 4:5); *"do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance"* (1 Peter 1:14). Against deceitful desires stands a mind made new: *"to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self"* (Ephesians 4:23–24). Against passions that pass stands the will of God, which lasts: *"so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God. For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do"* (1 Peter 4:2–3); *"the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life … the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever"* (1 John 2:16–17). And there is a share in his nature: *"partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire"* (2 Peter 1:4).

Desire can be evil in itself. "The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes" (Proverbs 21:10). "The wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the Lord" (Psalm 10:3). In Micah's day "the great man utters the evil desire of his soul; thus they weave it together" (Micah 7:3). God meets it from the other side: "The Lord does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked" (Proverbs 10:3). The sluggard's want gets nothing: "The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied" (Proverbs 13:4). And "Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way" (Proverbs 19:2).

Wanting can end in death. James gives the order: "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Wanting is also measured against death. Of the arrogant man, "His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Habakkuk 2:5). And "love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6).

A thirst met can be forgotten. *"You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst … But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck"*; they *"were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them"* (Nehemiah 9:15–17). Isaiah sets the same memory beside the wicked: *"They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock … There is no peace, says the Lord, for the wicked"* (Isaiah 48:21–22). I read a want met so fully that it was no longer felt, and the giver forgotten with it (10.3).

**Envy of what the wicked have.** Psalm 73 starts with its conclusion, "Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart" (73:1). Then it tells how near the psalmist came to losing it: "But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:2–3). Envy comes in by sight, as desire does. Thinking about it wore him out until he went "into the sanctuary of God" (73:16–17; 10.4, 10.9). There the prosperity was seen again: "Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms" (73:20). What he envied is a dream, and God's rousing is the waking. Then he names what envy had done to him: "When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you" (73:21–22). I read envy as a sight of another's good that embitters the soul. The psalm does not cure it with a better argument. It cures it with another seeing, in God's presence. Proverbs gives the same answer as a command, and sets it in time: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the Lord all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 23:17–18). Envy looks at what the other has now. The answer looks to "a future".

Envy can be pictured in a figure. Of the great tree that stands for Assyria, God says, *"I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it"* (Ezekiel 31:9). The next verse turns to the tree's own heart: *"its heart was proud of its height"* (31:10). I read the envy of the others and the pride of the tree as two answers to the same given beauty (Chapter 12).

**Jealousy among people who would be counted wise.** "Who is wise and understanding among you? … But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:13–16). "Bitter" is a taste, as "embittered" was for Asaph. It is "in your hearts", and outwardly it is "disorder". The middle word of James's three, "unspiritual", is literally "soulish".

What is precious can be a refuge. God lays *"a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste'"* (Isaiah 28:16). He says it to scoffers who had made another refuge: *"we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter"* (28:15). The one who believes is not hurried. Peter takes up the stone, *"a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6), and adds, *"So the honor is for you who believe"* (2:7).

A choice can be left wholly to God. David, fleeing Absalom, sends the ark back: "If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him" (2 Samuel 15:25–26). The act is yielding. He does not presume God's pleasure, and he does not keep the ark to secure it (13.1).

Fear is learned there too, at a meal: *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (Deuteronomy 14:23). In the same passage the people spend their money *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves"*, and *"eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). Fear of the Lord, a satisfied appetite and joy belong to the one meal, and the passage does not set them against each other. When a case is *"too difficult for you"*, the decision is sought at the place, and what is asked is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:8, 10). Presumption is the opposite, and its end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage names the limit and the carefulness, not the struggle.

Company is chosen too: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (Proverbs 16:19). And a whole way: "to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). Humility is in 10.14.

**Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).

Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them.
- At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20).
- With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21).
- With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7).
- In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32).
- Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17).
- Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13).
- A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7).
The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.

**The will made absolute.** Of Nebuchadnezzar: *"Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled"* (Daniel 5:19). The next verse says what happened inside him: *"But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down"* (5:20). He had been offered counsel (4:27). He was driven out *"until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will"* (5:21). His reason returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven (4:34). His son knew all this, and Daniel says to him, *"you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this"* (5:22). Knowing did not move his will.

The will made absolute is seen from below as well. "a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken" (Daniel 11:3–4). Another "shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him" (11:16), until "a commander shall put an end to his insolence" (11:18). Under such rulers a people says, "They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress" (Nehemiah 9:37), and says it of kings set over them "because of our sins" (Nehemiah 9:37). The same prayer remembers the land given "that they might do with them as they would" (9:24), and what followed: "they ate and were filled … Nevertheless, they were disobedient" (9:25–26). Of Elijah: "they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands" (Matthew 17:12).

**Doing the will of God.** The verses speak of God's will as something a person prays, knows, does, or fails to do.
- **Prayed.** "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10). At Gethsemane, the second time: "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done" (26:42), after "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays.
- **Asked within.** "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). And: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (John 15:7). I read the two together: the asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words.
- **Known by willing it.** "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). The willing comes before the knowing. Paul was "appointed … to know his will" (Acts 22:14), and was asked at once, "And now why do you wait?" (22:16). "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17).
- **Known and not done.** "you … know his will and approve what is excellent" (Romans 2:18) is said to one who boasts in God and teaches others (2:17, 19–21). "And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47), more than the one who did not know (12:48).
- **Said, and not done.** "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Of two sons, one said "I will not, but afterward he changed his mind and went", the other "I will, sir, but did not go". "Which of the two did the will of his father?" (21:29–31). Jesus turns the changed mind toward belief: "you did not afterward change your minds and believe him" (21:32).
- **What it is, where the verses say.** "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (4:3), "not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:5). "that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people" (1 Peter 2:15). After confession, "do his will. Separate yourselves" (Ezra 10:11).
- **With suffering, and with endurance.** "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil" (1 Peter 3:17), and the next verse, "For Christ also suffered" (3:18). "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised" (Hebrews 10:36).
- **Those who do it.** "For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:50; Mark 3:35), said with his hand stretched toward his disciples. "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him" (John 9:31), said by the man who had been blind.
- **God working it in them.** "equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight" (Hebrews 13:21). God "works in you, both to will and to work" (Philippians 2:13; 10.12). The renewed mind discerns "what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2; Chapter 14). Angels do it too (13.2).
- *Why:* what is refused, and for whose sake. Each passage gives its reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, pride.

When Scripture judges a person, it often names the heart. The heart is upright or crooked, pure or deceitful, whole or double, proud or humble. God "weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). The soul is the one who answers for what is done: "the soul who sins shall die". The spirit is judged too: haughty or lowly, crushed or contrite. Chapter 12 takes this further.

- **Thinking done in his presence sees differently.** "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). What he had been thinking about was envy: "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3). In the sanctuary he sees it as "a dream when one awakes" (73:20; 10.6, *Jealousy and envy*).

When God comes near, people are afraid, and they say why. At Sinai they asked that God not speak to them, "lest we die" (Exodus 20:19). Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6). In Zion the godless ask, "Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire?" (Isaiah 33:14). Job says, "I could not have faced his majesty" (Job 31:23). Each time the reason given is that they cannot stand before him.

The psalmist names two kinds of sin and asks differently for each. "Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression" (Psalm 19:12–13). Only the sins done knowingly are spoken of as able to rule him, and from those he asks to be held back. Elsewhere, in the same breath as longing for the commandments: "Keep steady my steps according to your promise, and let no iniquity get dominion over me. Redeem me from man's oppression, that I may keep your precepts" (Psalm 119:133–134). Two dominions stand side by side, sin within and oppression without, and he asks God against both (Chapter 14 for sin's rule ended).

A king was told that his kingdom would stand "from the time that you know that Heaven rules", with the counsel "break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed" (Daniel 4:26–27; 10.7, Chapter 4). The psalmist, given dominion over the works of God's hands, answers with wonder: "what is man that you are mindful of him", and "O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!" (Psalm 8:4, 9).

section: Care, discouragement and hiding between people
text:
What one person carries inside can be for another, or done to another.
- **Care for another is a good anxiety.** Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" is to be weak with the weak (2 Corinthians 11:28–29). Members of one body are to "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). Section 10.1 sets out the difference between this care and anxiety for oneself.
- **Losing heart is done by another.** "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Every use of the words for losing heart has another party behind it (10.1).
- **A whisperer separates friends.** "A whisperer separates close friends" (Proverbs 16:28), and "where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20) (10.5).
- **People hide from people, and hide one another.** The weaker side hides: "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). Rahab and Obadiah hid others to keep them alive (Joshua 2:4; 1 Kings 18:4). And no one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal" (Psalm 55:12–13). Section 10.11 follows all of this.

Much of what Scripture says about anger is about anger between people.
- **Kinship stops strife, or feeds it.** Abram: "Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kinsmen" (Genesis 13:8). He gave Lot the choice. In another quarrel, kinship is the weapon: "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter?" (2 Samuel 19:42). And "a brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city" (Proverbs 18:19).
- **Anger at a brother is judged like murder, and worship waits on peace.** "Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment … First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift" (Matthew 5:22, 24).
- **The anger of the powerful decides others' fate.** "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion" (Proverbs 19:12). Those under it plead (Genesis 44:18), read it as a sign ("if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him", 1 Samuel 20:7), or reach it through a go-between (Acts 12:20). Its favour has a ground too: *"A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully"* (Proverbs 14:35); *"his favor is like dew on the grass"* (19:12).
- **The law allows for heat.** The cities of refuge exist *"lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past"* (Deuteronomy 19:6). The Hebrew is literally "while his heart is hot". The law does not deny the grief. It puts a distance between the heat and the act, because the heat will not tell the innocent from the guilty.
- **The oppressor's wrath is shown with its end in view.** The king of Babylon "ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution" (Isaiah 14:6). The taunt over him begins "How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!" (14:4), and ends "The whole earth is at rest and quiet" (14:7).
- **A leader's anger can yield to a reason.** Moses was angry at Aaron's sons. When Aaron explained, "when Moses heard that, he approved" (Leviticus 10:20).
- **Anger is learned.** "Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare" (Proverbs 22:24–25).
- **Strife has a source inside.** "Your passions are at war within you" (James 4:1). Chapter 10.6 follows that.
- **It wears a household down.** "It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife" (Proverbs 21:9). The image is "a continual dripping on a rainy day" (27:15): duration, not a storm.
- **The one attacked feels it inside.** "In anger they bear a grudge against me. My heart is in anguish within me" (Psalm 55:3–4).
- **The trembling word is used of quarrel and rage.** Joseph sends his brothers home with "Do not quarrel on the way" (Genesis 45:24), and the word is *rāgaz*, "to tremble". "If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet" (Proverbs 29:9).
- **Love does not get provoked.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **One person's sin can bring trouble on many.** David, under the plague, asks to bear it alone: "these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house" (2 Samuel 24:17).
- **Vengeance is left to God.** "Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God … if your enemy is hungry, feed him" (Romans 12:19–20).

**It is aimed at the quiet and the weak.** The verses name who it is aimed at:
- *"In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor"* (Psalm 10:2)
- *"against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit"* (Psalm 35:20)
- *"The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him"* (Psalm 37:12)
- Gog: *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme and say, 'I will go up against the land of unwalled villages. I will fall upon the quiet people who dwell securely'"* (Ezekiel 38:10–11)

Between people, humility is a way of counting the other: "in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others" (Philippians 2:3–4). It is set against "selfish ambition or conceit" (2:3), and against being "haughty" or "wise in your own sight" (Romans 12:16). It is worn toward others: "Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another" (1 Peter 5:5). And it is named beside "bearing with one another in love" (Ephesians 4:2).

People hold wishes about one another, and Paul fears what disappointment would bring: *"For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder"* (2 Corinthians 12:20). Each side has a wish about the other. I read expectation between people as the ground on which quarrel and jealousy grow, named by the one who fears it.

In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).
- Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).
- Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.
- At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).

And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.
- The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).
- No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

A friendly word can be the cover. *"Come and let us meet together"*, Sanballat wrote, *"But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). Jeremiah did not see it at all: *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). The psalmist names the arrogant who *"have hidden a trap for me"* (Psalm 140:5). 10.10 (*Plotting against another*) follows what passes between them.

section: Fear that comes upon a person
text:
Terror can also come as an event, from outside.
- It strikes: "I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm" (Proverbs 1:26–27). Wisdom is the speaker. The same speech says they "did not choose the fear of the Lord" (1:29). I read the passage as setting the fear of the Lord, not chosen, beside the terror that comes.
- It comes where peace was looked for: "We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror" (Jeremiah 8:15).
- It is given in the curse: "the Lord will give you there a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul" (Deuteronomy 28:65). The mind itself is struck: "The Lord will strike you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind" (Deuteronomy 28:28).
- It can come where there is nothing to fear: "There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror!" (Psalm 53:5).

Fear of God is also called for as a guard, and set against pride. "So do not become proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you" (Romans 11:20–21). "Let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it" (Hebrews 4:1).

Fear of other people takes several forms in the verses.
- **Fear of man.** "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies" (Isaiah 51:12). "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
- **Fear for another.** Eli trembled for the ark (1 Samuel 4:13). Jeremiah grieved for his people: "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21). Paul: "I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3).
- **Fear used as a tool.** "he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin" (Nehemiah 6:13).
- **Respect owed.** The same word as fear is rendered "respect" toward people. "respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed" (Romans 13:7). "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1 Peter 2:18). Toward parents: "Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father" (Leviticus 19:3).
- **Respect and no fear, two verses apart.** "Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:14–15). In Greek, "fear" and "respect" are the same word. The verse does not say whether the respect is toward the one who asks or toward God.
- **Being feared.** Being feared works on the one who is feared. "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).

The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
- **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
- **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
- **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
- **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
- **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
- **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
- **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).

The English words anger, wrath, fury and indignation stand for many Hebrew and Greek words. Some are used of God and of people alike, and some are kept almost entirely for God.
- ***ʾAph*, "nostril, anger".** It is the commonest word. Its first sense is the nose, and the verses keep the picture: "pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife" (Proverbs 30:33). It is used of God's anger and of people's. It is also the word of *slow to anger*, which is literally long of nostril.
- ***Ḥēmāh*, "heat, wrath".** It is poured and kindled: "Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah" (Jeremiah 44:6). The same word is the venom of the serpent: "They have venom like the venom of a serpent" (Psalm 58:4). It is also the heat of wine: "the princes became sick with the heat of wine" (Hosea 7:5).
- ***Ḥārāh*, "to burn", and *ḥārôn*, "burning".** The verb is used of people and of God. The noun, *fierce anger*, is God's every time it is anger. Many of its verses speak of it turning: "Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people" (Exodus 32:12).
- ***Kāʿas*, "to provoke, vex".** As a verb it is mostly people provoking God (Deuteronomy 4:25). As a noun it is mostly what a person carries: Hannah's "great anxiety and vexation" (1 Samuel 1:16), "Sorrow is better than laughter" (Ecclesiastes 7:3). One word covers provoking God and Hannah's grief.
- ***Qeṣep̄* and *zaʿam*, "wrath" and "indignation".** These are almost always God's. *Zaʿam* names a period with an end: "the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end" (Daniel 8:19).
- ***ʿEbrāh*, "overflow, wrath".** It is God's wrath, and it is also pride that overflows: "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24).
- ***Zāʿap̄*, "rage".** It is Uzziah's anger (2 Chronicles 26:19), and also a troubled face: "Why are your faces downcast today?" (Genesis 40:7).
- **The Greek words.** *Orgē*, "wrath", is God's in most of its uses. The same noun is the anger people are told to put away (Colossians 3:6, 8). *Orgizō*, "to be angry", is never God's own anger. *Thymos*, "passion, wrath", is God's, people's and the devil's. *Aganakteō*, "to be indignant", is used of Jesus, the disciples and the religious leaders. *Paroxynō*, "to provoke", is both a spirit "provoked within him" (Acts 17:16) and "stir up one another to love" (Hebrews 10:24).

The proverbs set the one who turns anger away beside the one who stirs it: "Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath" (Proverbs 29:8). The scoffer's words set a whole city alight. Three verses on: "A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back" (29:11). I read the wise man who turns another's wrath away as the same man who holds back his own.

The verses name a cause each time.
- **A covenant broken:** "So the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he said, 'Because this people have transgressed my covenant'" (Judges 2:20).
- **Complaint heard:** "When the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled" (Numbers 11:1).
- **Unwilling to listen:** "But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me … Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them" (Ezekiel 20:8). The next verse holds it back: "But I acted for the sake of my name" (20:9).
- **A hardened hearing:** "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came from the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 7:12).
- **Pride:** "his heart was proud. Therefore wrath came upon him and Judah and Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 32:25).
- **Messengers mocked:** "they kept mocking the messengers of God … until the wrath of the Lord rose against his people, until there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16).
- **What is done to the weak:** "If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exodus 22:23–24).
- **The truth held down:** "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Romans 1:18).

section: The heart that turns, and the heart that does not
text: Josiah heard the book read and tore his clothes. The answer named his heart: "because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the Lord … I also have heard you" (2 Kings 22:19). Hezekiah's "heart was proud", and wrath came. "But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart … so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). The same heart provoked the anger and turned it.

section: The heart that turns, and the heart that does not
text: And some cover the danger over with false peace. "You say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me'" (Jeremiah 2:35). Prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'" (Jeremiah 23:17). John the Baptist meets the same thing: "do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father'" (Matthew 3:9).

At the end, the reverse: people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb'" (Revelation 6:16). One shelter is in God; the other is from him. Isaiah: "Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "when he rises to terrify the earth" (2:19).

Some people carry out God's anger, and the verses judge how they do it.
- **Assyria is the rod, and has its own heart:** "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger … But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isaiah 10:5, 7). He boasts, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom" (10:13), and the Lord "will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes" (10:12). "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it …?" (10:15).
- **Babylon goes too far:** "I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy" (Isaiah 47:6). "While I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **Israel's army goes past the commission:** "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2 Chronicles 28:9).
- **Saul is judged for not carrying it out:** "Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the Lord has done this thing to you this day" (1 Samuel 28:18).
- **The governing authority:** "he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer. Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience" (Romans 13:4–5).

The verses show anger changing character with its circumstances.
- **Who is angry.** The same words are used for God and for people, and "for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9) is said in restraint.
- **Whether what sets it off is true.** Potiphar acted on a lie (Genesis 39:19).
- **For whom it burns.** For the widow and fatherless (Exodus 22:24); for the children (Mark 10:14); for one wronged (2 Samuel 12:5).
- **What it is joined with in the verse.** Jealousy (Deuteronomy 6:15); grief, "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5); the Spirit (1 Samuel 11:6); hatred, "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred" (Ezekiel 35:11); fear, "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged" (Daniel 11:30); compassion set against it (Hosea 11:8–9).
- **Time.** God's "for a moment" (Psalm 30:5) and "finished" (Revelation 15:1); a man's wrath kept "forever" (Amos 1:11); "do not let the sun go down on your anger" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Power.** The ruler's anger becomes a command (Daniel 2:12).
- **The one who carries it out,** and their own heart (Isaiah 10:7).
- **One and many** (Numbers 16:22; Joshua 7:1).
- **What meets it.** A soft answer, a servants' question, a father who comes out, a counsellor (Proverbs 15:1; 2 Kings 5:13; Luke 15:28; Acts 5:34–35). Or no one: "I looked, but there was no one to help" (Isaiah 63:5).
- **Correction with or without the anger:** "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24).
- **The measure:** "storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *ʿEbrāh* is wrath and pride (Proverbs 21:24). *Kāʿas* is provoking God and Hannah's grief (1 Samuel 1:16). *Ḥēmāh* is wrath and venom (Psalm 140:3). *Paroxysmos* is a sharp disagreement and stirring up to love (Acts 15:39; Hebrews 10:24). *Thymos* is God's wrath and Babylon's passion (Revelation 14:8, 10).

Humility is not a feeling in the verses. In none that I read is a person said to feel humble. They speak of it in other ways:
- **as something a person does.** He humbles himself, before God or before God's word.
- **as a standing.** Some are called the humble, the lowly or the meek.
- **as something sought and walked in.** "Seek humility" (Zephaniah 2:3). "Walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8).
- **as a state of the spirit.** A lowly and contrite spirit; a broken heart.
- **as a place taken among people.** The lower seat; counting others more significant than oneself.
- **as something done to a person.** God humbles to test and to teach, and he brings the proud low.
- **as God's own way.** He "looks far down" (Psalm 113:6), and in his Son he "humbled himself" (Philippians 2:8).

In every one of these the verses set humility against a rising: the proud heart, the lifted-up self, the stiff neck, the haughty eyes. I cannot read humility in Scripture without reading what it stands against. Chapter 12 holds pride, and this section holds its counterpart.

Hebrew has a verb for humbling oneself or being humbled, used also when a nation is "subdued" in war. It has another for bringing low, used of the proud, of mountains and of a city. It has a word for the lowly, and one word that is translated "humble", "afflicted", "meek" and "poor" by turns. The same Hebrew word stands behind "the humble" whom God teaches (Psalm 25:9), "the afflicted" whose cry he does not forget (Psalm 9:12), "the meek" who inherit the land (Psalm 37:11), and Moses, "very meek" (Numbers 12:3). The English changes with what the verse is about. The Hebrew does not.

The verses place it in the heart.
- "Because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the Lord" (2 Kings 22:19), or, in the parallel account, "your heart was tender" (2 Chronicles 34:27).
- "If then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity" (Leviticus 26:41), after they "confess their iniquity" (26:40).
- "Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:26). The verse before says, "his heart was proud" (32:25). I read this as the same heart turning back from itself. The pride and the humbling are in one place.
- Daniel's is not a response to rebuke at all: "from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard" (Daniel 10:12). Here humbling oneself stands beside setting the heart to understand.

Jesus gives it a face. The tax collector, "standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner!'" The Pharisee beside him prayed, "God, I thank you that I am not like other men … I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get." Jesus: "this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 18:11–14). The one who lifts himself measures himself against others and lists what he does. The one who humbles himself owns that he is a sinner and asks for mercy.
- pride of heart (2 Chronicles 32:25–26)
- "you have lifted up yourself against the Lord" (Daniel 5:23), as with his father: "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly" (5:20)

When Hezekiah's couriers carried the call, the cities "laughed them to scorn and mocked them. However, some men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 30:10–11). The same call met two hearts. The verses do not say why.

section: A humbling God does not take knowledge of
text: The New Testament names the same thing. The noun for humility appears as "asceticism": "Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism … puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind", and "self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:18, 23). What looks like lowering puffs the person up. The Pharisee's "I fast twice a week" stands on the same side (Luke 18:12).

**To show the heart, and to teach.** "that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not. And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna … that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone" (Deuteronomy 8:2–3). The end is named: "to do you good in the end" (8:16). The danger it guards against comes in the same chapter. When plenty comes, "your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord", and you "say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (8:14, 17). The next chapter goes on: "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (9:4).
**Against pride.** "those who walk in pride he is able to humble", said by Nebuchadnezzar after his reason returned (Daniel 4:37). The humbled man says it of what was done to him.

section: The proud brought low, the lowly raised
text:
